commentary.bottom_line: No study in this map tests whether disclosing AI-generated text, disclosing AI use in methods, or following AI reporting guidelines improves readers' ability to judge AI's role or validity in published research. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and commentary alone.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Among the listed endorsements, two are guidance documents and ten are commentaries, all phrased as "should." Consensus of this kind cannot be rated for effect, so the certainty that disclosure or guideline adherence changes reader appraisal or research validity remains unassessed.

The endorsers point to existing journal and reporting norms rather than law. They name CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI for trial reporting and ICMJE, WAME, and COPE policies on AI disclosure and authorship. These norms depend on journal enforcement, and the supplied material contains no data on compliance or on penalties for undisclosed AI use.

commentary.research_gap: Studies could compare manuscripts with and without structured AI-use statements or reporting-guideline checklists and measure whether reviewers and readers detect AI-related errors, assess validity more accurately, or reproduce results more often. Audits of adherence to CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI in published AI studies would also show whether the guidelines are followed in practice.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether disclosure requirements affect how research on AI tools for these populations is reported or appraised is unknown.
